plain: Stale beans are one of the most common culprits; coffee starts losing flavor within a couple weeks of roasting, so beans that have been sitting around for months will taste flat and dull no matter how well you brew them. Grind size mismatched to your brewing method is another frequent issue: too fine for a French press causes over-extraction and bitterness, while too coarse for espresso leads to weak, sour shots. Water quality matters more than people expect, since coffee is over 98% water, so heavily chlorinated or mineral-heavy tap water can introduce off-flavors. Incorrect water temperature, ideally between 195-205°F, can under-extract if too cool, tasting sour, or over-extract if too hot, tasting bitter and harsh. Finally, dirty equipment, with old coffee oils building up in your grinder or machine, can introduce rancid flavors that taint even perfectly good beans.

plain: The transition from prehistory to history is generally marked by the invention and adoption of writing, since history as a discipline relies on written records to reconstruct events, while prehistory refers to everything before written documentation existed. This means the exact dividing line varies by region, since writing developed at very different times: Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3200 BCE, China around 1200 BCE, and some cultures not until European contact centuries later, meaning parts of the world were still prehistoric while others had been literate for millennia. This is why the terms 'prehistoric' and 'historic' are considered relative rather than universal fixed dates, and archaeologists rely heavily on other evidence, like tools and physical remains, to study prehistoric societies since no written records exist for them.

plain: The 'Golden Age of Rome' most commonly refers to the reign of Augustus, the first Roman emperor, who ruled from 27 BCE to 14 CE and ushered in the Pax Romana, roughly two centuries of relative peace, stability, and prosperity across the empire after decades of civil war. Either way, the phrase generally points to Rome at the height of its cultural achievement and internal stability.
